response.title: solar power for a chicken coop with a heated waterer
response.answer:
You can absolutely run a chicken coop with a solar-powered heated waterer, but the biggest challenge is keeping the water from freezing overnight, when the solar panels aren't producing electricity.

For a typical backyard chicken coop, I'd recommend a 12V or 24V solar system with a LiFePO4 battery, rather than a small all-in-one solar kit.

Recommended solar setup

STARTING POINT · HEATED WATERER + SMALL COOP

Solar panels

400–600W

Battery

200Ah

12.8V LiFePO4

Waterer heater

40–100W

Charge controller

MPPT
Preliminary sizing for a modest winter climate. Actual requirements depend heavily on temperature, heater duty cycle, and winter sunlight.

The battery stores solar energy during the day and powers the heated waterer overnight. A thermostat-controlled waterer is particularly helpful because it only draws power when heat is needed.

How much electricity will it need?

Here's an example using a 60W heated waterer.

Heater operating hours per day

12h

Mild weather

Continuous heating

Daily heater consumption

0.72 kWh

Approx. 200Ah battery runtime

2.8 days
Assumes 80% of nominal battery energy reaches the heater, no solar recharging, and no other loads. Actual thermostat cycling varies with weather.
Example equipment

Farm Innovators Heated Poultry Drinker, 2-gal

60W thermostatic, 2-gallon waterer

$54.99

HQST 400W 12V RV Solar Kit with 200Ah LiFePO4 Battery

400W solar kit with 200Ah battery; verify inverter is included

$884.99

For a 120V waterer, you'll also need a properly sized pure-sine-wave inverter, appropriate fuses, weather-protected wiring, and GFCI protection. The manufacturer's safety instructions specifically require GFCI protection. 
premier1supplies.com

If the battery can get below freezing, choose a model with low-temperature charge protection or self-heating.

Three questions so I can size your system accurately
1. How cold does it get in winter?
20–32°F (mild freezing)
0–20°F (cold)
Below 0°F (very cold)
Rarely below freezing
2. What do you want solar to power?
Heated waterer only
Heated waterer + LED lights
Waterer + lights + automatic door
3. How many chickens?
Calculate my solar setup

With these details, I can work out whether a smaller, cheaper solar system will be sufficient or whether you'll need the full 400–600W setup.

For a typical backyard chicken coop, I'd recommend a **12V or 24V solar system with a LiFePO4 battery**, rather than a small all-in-one solar kit.

## Recommended solar setup

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">STARTING POINT · HEATED WATERER + SMALL COOP</text>
  <grid columns={2} gap={3}>
    <grid-item>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">Solar panels</text>
      <title size="xl" color="default">400–600W</title>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">Battery</text>
      <title size="xl" color="default">200Ah</title>
      <text color="tertiary" size="2xs">12.8V LiFePO4</text>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">Waterer heater</text>
      <title size="xl" color="default">40–100W</title>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">Charge controller</text>
      <title size="xl" color="default">MPPT</title>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <caption>Preliminary sizing for a modest winter climate. Actual requirements depend heavily on temperature, heater duty cycle, and winter sunlight.</caption>
</box>

The battery stores solar energy during the day and powers the heated waterer overnight. A thermostat-controlled waterer is particularly helpful because it only draws power when heat is needed.

## How much electricity will it need?

Here's an example using a 60W heated waterer.

{@body const [hours,setHours] = DIL.useState(12)}
{@body const wh=60*hours}
<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **Heater operating hours per day**
    <title size="lg" tabularNums>{hours}h</title>
  </row>
  <slider min={2} max={24} step={2} value={hours} onChange={setHours}/>
  <row justify="between">
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Mild weather</text>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Continuous heating</text>
  </row>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <grid columns={2} gap={3}>
    <grid-item>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">Daily heater consumption</text>
      <title size="xl" color="default" tabularNums>{(wh/1000).toFixed(2)} kWh</title>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">Approx. 200Ah battery runtime</text>
      <title size="xl" color="default" tabularNums>{Math.round(2560*0.8/(60*hours)*10)/10} days</title>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <caption>Assumes 80% of nominal battery energy reaches the heater, no solar recharging, and no other loads. Actual thermostat cycling varies with weather.</caption>
</box>

## Example equipment

<box gap={3}>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <AsyncImage ref="turn198699product4" maxWidth="116px" aspectRatio="1:1" shop_eligible={true}/>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **<Entity ref="turn198699product4" category="product" value={turn198699product4.title}/>**
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">60W thermostatic, 2-gallon waterer</text>
      <text weight="medium">{turn198699product4.displayed_price}</text>
    </box>
  </row>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <AsyncImage ref="turn198699product1" maxWidth="116px" aspectRatio="1:1" shop_eligible={true}/>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **<Entity ref="turn198699product1" category="product" value={turn198699product1.title}/>**
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">400W solar kit with 200Ah battery; verify inverter is included</text>
      <text weight="medium">{turn198699product1.displayed_price}</text>
    </box>
  </row>
</box>

For a 120V waterer, you'll also need a properly sized pure-sine-wave inverter, appropriate fuses, weather-protected wiring, and GFCI protection. The manufacturer's safety instructions specifically require GFCI protection. <Cite ref="turn198699search12"/>

If the battery can get below freezing, choose a model with low-temperature charge protection or self-heating.

## Three questions so I can size your system accurately

{@body const [climate,setClimate] = DIL.useState("20–32°F")}
{@body const [power,setPower] = DIL.useState("Waterer + lights")}
{@body const [chickens,setChickens] = DIL.useState("6")}
<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <form gap={3} onSubmit={()=>GenUI.issueNewTurn("Design a solar power system for my chicken coop. Lowest winter temperature: "+climate+". Power needs: "+power+". Number of chickens: "+chickens+". Please provide panel and battery sizing, a parts list, and estimated total cost.")}>
    <box gap={1}>
      <label>1. How cold does it get in winter?</label>
      <radio-group direction="col" value={climate} onChange={setClimate}>
        <radio value="20–32°F">20–32°F (mild freezing)</radio>
        <radio value="0–20°F">0–20°F (cold)</radio>
        <radio value="Below 0°F">Below 0°F (very cold)</radio>
        <radio value="Rarely below 32°F">Rarely below freezing</radio>
      </radio-group>
    </box>
    <divider color="subtle"/>
    <box gap={1}>
      <label>2. What do you want solar to power?</label>
      <radio-group direction="col" value={power} onChange={setPower}>
        <radio value="Heated waterer only">Heated waterer only</radio>
        <radio value="Waterer + lights">Heated waterer + LED lights</radio>
        <radio value="Waterer + lights + automatic door">Waterer + lights + automatic door</radio>
      </radio-group>
    </box>
    <divider color="subtle"/>
    <box gap={1}>
      <label>3. How many chickens?</label>
      <input value={chickens} onChange={setChickens} placeholder="e.g. 6" inputType="number"/>
    </box>
    <button block submit>Calculate my solar setup <icon name="arrow-right" inline/></button>
  </form>
</box>

With these details, I can work out whether a smaller, cheaper solar system will be sufficient or whether you'll need the full 400–600W setup.
